title: How Bounty Hunters Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explore how bounty hunters (bail enforcement agents) work after a bail skip, following up on the prior bail bonds episode. They cover the Old West origins and the 1873 Taylor v. Taintor case, bounty hunter Bob Burton's stories and earnings, the ten percent bail premium and how bondsmen get paid, the broad powers bounty hunters have under bail contracts (no warrants needed, no Miranda, extradition waivers), states like Kentucky, Illinois and Oregon that restrict them, the Andrew Luster capture in Mexico and Dog the Bounty Hunter, tactics such as stakeouts, surveillance, pretexting and finding the "Judas," the rules on freelancing versus exclusive work with one bondsman, weapons and licensing, and how to become a bounty hunter. The episode ends with an official apology to Jehovah's Witnesses over a prior listener mail segment about a blood transfusion, and a listener email from James K in Calgary, Alberta.

segments.title: Opening banter and bail skipping intro
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the two-part bail follow-up, mention the MPR bail series that inspired it, and tease the question of what happens when you skip bail: a bounty hunter gets sent after you.

segments.title: History of bounty hunting and Taylor v. Taintor
segments.summary: The hosts trace the term to the Old West and an 1873 Supreme Court case, Taylor v. Taintor, which gave bounty hunters authority as agents for bail bondsmen. They note Old West dead-or-alive wanted posters and Jesse James's bounty.

segments.title: Bob Burton and bounty hunter earnings
segments.summary: Bob Burton, a well-known bounty hunter who reportedly made 20,000 arrests in 2007, is quoted on the thrill of the job. The hosts explain that bounty hunters typically earn about ten percent of the bail amount from the bondsman, and that experienced hunters can earn roughly fifty thousand to a hundred thousand dollars a year.

segments.title: How bail bonds and skipping work
segments.summary: Chuck recaps the bail bond process: the defendant pays a ten percent premium, the bondsman guarantees appearance, and if the defendant skips, the bondsman may owe the full bail and sends a bounty hunter. Bounty hunters and bondsmen are usually separate professions.

segments.title: Bounty hunter powers, limits, and state restrictions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the bail contract waivers that give bounty hunters broad powers, including no warrant needed, no Miranda, and waived extradition rights. They explain that bounty hunters are wary of roughing up suspects, that only a small fraction of suspects fight, and that Kentucky, Illinois and Oregon bar bounty hunters, requiring a court warrant in Kentucky.

segments.title: Mexico, Andrew Luster, and Dog the Bounty Hunter
segments.summary: The hosts describe the limits on crossing international borders, citing the capture of Andrew Luster in Mexico by Dog the Bounty Hunter. Mexico later dropped charges after a letter on Luster's behalf, and Dog's TV show continued.

segments.title: Stakeouts, tactics, and the Judas
segments.summary: The hosts describe investigative tactics: records and phone checks, street asking, stakeouts, pinhole cameras, surprise and disguise, rigging a suspect's car lock, and finding a 'Judas' who has a grudge against the fugitive.

segments.title: Licensing, weapons, freelancing, and becoming a bounty hunter
segments.summary: The hosts discuss gun licensing requirements, state rules on freelance bounty hunters versus exclusive work for one bondsman (Florida, North Carolina and South Carolina cited), the risks to a bounty hunter's family, and how to get training through emerging degree programs.

segments.title: Apology to Jehovah's Witnesses and listener email
segments.summary: The hosts officially apologize to Jehovah's Witnesses for how a prior listener mail segment about a blood transfusion came across. They then read an email from James K in Calgary, Alberta, who has binged the podcast and asks for more episodes.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck close with listener email instructions and website pointers, then the episode ends.
